screens.title: Optimizing HDAs for Real-time Performance and Baking
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why performance must be a first-class concern when authoring Houdini Digital Assets for games. We’ll define the core metrics you will monitor — polygon count, draw calls, and texture memory — and show how a procedural HDA can unintentionally exceed budgets if nodes like subdivision, many booleans, or dense VDB conversions are used without restraint. You will see practical strategies for streamlining node graphs, using PolyReduce and Clean to reduce geometry and attribute overhead, and how to bake or cache stable outputs with ROP Geometry Output and File Cache to avoid expensive cooks at runtime. We’ll also cover baking attribute maps — for example turning a procedural moss density attribute into a grayscale texture — and why clean UVs and normals matter before exporting to a game engine. Finally, we’ll outline HDA design best practices: modularity, clear parameters, LOD support, and providing collision geometry. By the end you’ll understand both the techniques and the trade-offs needed to produce HDAs that are flexible for artists and light enough for real-time engines.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify the primary performance metrics that matter for real-time assets, optimize HDA internals to reduce geometry and attribute overhead, and bake stable outputs for game engines. You’ll learn to use PolyReduce, Clean, Fuse, and Attribute Delete to shape geometry and memory usage, and you’ll practice exporting baked geometry using ROP Geometry Output or File Cache for reliable engine imports. You’ll also learn how to bake attribute-driven masks and utility maps so procedural data can become practical texture inputs in the engine. Each objective pairs a technical skill with a practical reason: reducing polygons keeps frame rates steady; baking avoids expensive cooks inside the engine; and clean UVs plus proper normals make materials behave predictably. As you practice, you’ll compare common mistakes — like overusing subdivide nodes — with better alternatives so you build an HDA that balances control and runtime cost.

screens.title: Performance Metrics: Polygon Count, Draw Calls, Texture Memory
screens.narratorSegment: Performance for game assets is not an abstract goal — it is a set of measurable constraints. Polygon count is the total number of polygons your mesh contains and directly affects G P U throughput. Draw calls are how many times the C P U needs to instruct the G P U to render geometry; many separate meshes or material changes increase draw calls. Texture memory is the combined size of your texture maps and controls G P U memory usage. When designing an HDA, think in budgets: an HDA that outputs many separate primitives or high-resolution textures will consume more of these limits. A concrete example: a procedural tree HDA that generates highly detailed leaves with per-leaf meshes will skyrocket poly count and draw calls compared to a card-based sprite solution. A common misconception is assuming procedural flexibility automatically translates to runtime performance — it does not. Procedural generation is powerful while authoring, but what matters at runtime is the final baked geometry and assets the engine receives. Key takeaway: always measure the outputs your HDA produces in terms of triangles, number of objects/material groups, and texture sizes, and set target values that match your platform. A practical check is to ask: can I reduce the mesh or combine material groups without losing the visual goal? That question guides the optimization choices you’ll make later in the workflow.

keyIdea.title: Measure first

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Performance Metrics
Definitions & Why They Matter
  • Polygon Count: Number of triangles in the mesh; higher counts increase GPU load.
  • Draw Calls: Number of separate draw operations; many meshes or materials raise CPU overhead.
  • Texture Memory: Size of texture assets loaded to GPU; large maps increase VRAM usage.
Common Mistake
Relying on procedural detail alone and forgetting that the engine uses the final baked mesh; procedural is for authoring, not always for runtime.
Concrete Example
Imagine an HDA that generates a cluster of rocks with per-rock micro-detail. You can either keep each rock as full geometry, which increases draw calls and polygons, or bake normal/detail maps and merge meshes to lower draw calls while preserving visual fidelity.
High Detail
Many meshes • High polygon count • High draw calls
Optimized
Merged meshes • Reduced polys • Baked maps
Key Takeaway

Measure what your HDA emits, and design to match the engine’s polygon, draw-call, and texture budgets.

screens.title: Streamlining HDA Networks: Practical Optimization Steps
screens.narratorSegment: Optimizing an HDA begins with a disciplined pass through its internal network. Start by identifying redundant or unused nodes: delete unnecessary SOPs, merge equivalent flows, and remove attributes that are no longer used. A useful process is: first profile the HDA by observing cook times and the viewport's geometry stats; second, replace expensive nodes or reduce their parameters (for example reduce Subdivide iterations); third, promote important controls like the PolyReduce target to the HDA interface so artists can trade quality for performance. A concrete example: if your HDA performs multiple overlapping boolean operations, try precomputing the boolean result in a cached branch and using a single, cleaned output for all subsequent steps. Another practical step is attribute hygiene — use Attribute Delete to strip attributes like temporary masks or per-point IDs before exporting. A common misconception is believing that more nodes always give more control; in practice, a dense graph with many intermediate results slows cooks and complicates debugging. Key takeaway: optimize both the topology of the node graph and the data it carries by pruning nodes and attributes, and provide a small set of well-documented parameters to control remaining detail.

keyIdea.title: Optimization process
keyIdea.text: Profile, prune, parameterize: remove wasted nodes and attributes, and expose only the controls artists need.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Streamlining Networks
Optimization Steps
  1. Profile cooks and identify slow nodes or heavy SOPs.
  2. Remove or collapse redundant nodes and branches.
  3. Replace expensive operations or reduce their parameters (e.g., Subdivide iterations).
  4. Use Attribute Delete to remove unneeded attributes before export.
  5. Expose a small set of LOD parameters to the HDA interface.
Pro tip
Expose PolyReduce target as a slider so final quality can be adjusted per platform without modifying the network.
Example Scenario
A building HDA had multiple decorative boolean cuts and per-brick procedural bevels. By caching the combined boolean result, deleting temporary group attributes, and running a single PolyReduce with a promoted parameter, cook time dropped and exported geometry fit the engine budget.
Common Mistake

Leaving many intermediate attributes and temporary groups increases memory usage and file size. Delete them before exporting.

screens.title: PolyReduce vs. Other Cleanup Nodes
screens.narratorSegment: PolyReduce is your primary tool for lowering polygon count while attempting to preserve silhouette and visual fidelity. It is optimal when you need to decimate dense meshes intelligently. However, it is not a one-stop solution: Fuse is useful to merge overlapping points and reduce vertex count, while Clean removes unused groups, attributes, and degenerate geometry that can silently bloat exports. Attribute Delete targets memory and file size by removing attributes that the game engine will not use. A concrete example: after decimating a scanned rock with PolyReduce, you should run Fuse to collapse nearly coincident points created by the simplification, run Clean to remove degenerate primitives, and then Attribute Delete to remove scan-specific attributes like raw color or per-vertex IDs. A common misconception is to over-rely on PolyReduce for all optimization; PolyReduce changes topology and can destroy UV layouts if not configured properly. Key takeaway: use PolyReduce to control triangle budgets, then use Fuse, Clean, and Attribute Delete as a final hygiene pass to ensure exports are compact and engine-friendly. When you expose PolyReduce settings as an HDA parameter, document acceptable ranges so artists don’t exceed platform budgets.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › PolyReduce & Cleanup
Quick Comparison
PolyReduce
Decimate triangles with shape preservation; promote target percentage for artists.
Fuse
Merge near-coincident points to reduce vertex count after simplification.
Clean
Remove degenerate primitives and unused groups; fixes non-manifold issues.
Attribute Delete
Trim attributes that increase memory or are unnecessary in the engine.
Practical Sequence
  1. Run PolyReduce to hit triangle target.
  2. Run Fuse to collapse close points.
  3. Run Clean to remove degenerate geometry and groups.
  4. Run Attribute Delete to drop unused attributes before export.
Key Takeaway

PolyReduce sets the budget; Fuse, Clean and Attribute Delete enforce hygiene and export safety.

screens.title: Pre-baking and Export: ROP Geometry Output and File Cache
screens.narratorSegment: Baking is the practice of converting dynamic or expensive procedural results into static files that the engine can load quickly. Houdini provides the ROP Geometry Output node to export geometry directly to formats like FBX and the File Cache node to save networks as. bgeo. sc or other formats. A robust bake architecture separates outputs by purpose: visual mesh, collision mesh, and LOD meshes should each have a dedicated ROP or cache path. For example, connect the cleaned HDA output to a ROP Geometry Output node named with suffixes like _mesh, _collision, or _lod1 so your pipeline can import each file into the engine. Use File Cache for internal iteration — if an HDA takes 30 seconds to cook, caching that result to disk yields rapid iteration and avoids re-cooking heavy operations. A common misconception is that baking removes the need for version control; on the contrary, you should version baked outputs and keep the HDA definition under control too. Key takeaway: design bake outputs explicitly, separate functional exports, and automate file naming. This makes importing into the engine predictable and fast for runtime use.

keyIdea.title: Baking architecture
keyIdea.text: Export separate baked outputs for mesh, collision, and LODs using ROP Geometry Output and File Cache to speed iteration and engine imports.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Pre-baking & Export
Bake Patterns
Create dedicated outputs for each required file. Use consistent naming and folder structure so exported FBX or BGEO files map cleanly into the engine pipeline.
ROP Geometry Output
Use for exporting FBX/OBJ/Alembic. Configure Output File and SOP Path to target the cleaned SOP chain you want to export.
File Cache
Cache heavy computations locally as .bgeo.sc for fast iteration and to avoid re-cooking expensive nodes during development.
Example Export Paths
$HIP/geo/cohortia_simple_box_baked.fbx
$HIP/cache/cohortia_simple_box_cache.$F.bgeo.sc
$HIP/geo/rock_mesh_lod1.fbx
$HIP/geo/rock_collision.fbx
Use clear suffixes so engine importers pick the correct file for visuals, collisions or LODs.
Key Takeaway

Bake explicit outputs for each engine need and cache intermediate results to speed iteration and avoid re-cooks.

screens.title: Automating Exports: Practical Script Example
screens.narratorSegment: Automation reduces human error when setting up exports. The chapter includes a simple Python pattern to create a geometry container, a sphere and a null, and hook the sphere into the null. You can adapt this style to create a ROP or File Cache node and set its parameters programmatically. For example, a script that creates a geo container and inside it creates an FBX ROP lets you standardize output paths and SOP paths across many HDAs. A misconception is believing automation replaces thinking; instead, automation enforces consistent naming and reduces tedious setup. Concretely, you might create a script that: creates the geo node, builds the internal chain up to the Clean SOP, creates a ROP Geometry Output node, sets Output File to a predictable path, and triggers render. This ensures every artist exports with the same settings and reduces mistakes like forgetting to set the SOP Path. The takeaway: use small scripts to standardize exports but keep the logic simple and well-documented so others can adapt it without breaking pipeline conventions. In practical terms, a safe python pattern for creating nodes and wiring a simple export chain.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.text: Use small, documented scripts to create export nodes and set consistent file paths to reduce manual errors.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Automating Exports
Why Script Exports
Scripting standardizes output paths, SOP paths, and node creation. It saves time and ensures consistent export settings for teams.
Example (conceptual)
import hou
root = hou.node("/obj")
geo = root.createNode("geo","my_geo")
sphere = geo.createNode("sphere","mesh")
clean = geo.createNode("clean","clean_out")
clean.setInput(0, sphere)
rop = geo.createNode("rop_fbxoutput","export_fbx")
rop.parm("sop_path").set(clean.path())
rop.parm("output_file").set("$HIP/geo/my_geo_baked.fbx")
# Then trigger the rop render or save parameters for manual run
This snippet shows the pattern: create nodes, connect, set parameters, and export. Adapt to your HDA naming conventions.
Practical Note
Keep automation small and reversible. Make scripts set parameters but avoid destructive actions unless explicitly confirmed, and log created files for traceability.
Key Takeaway

Automate export setup to enforce consistent naming and reduce human error, but document and constrain scripts so they remain safe.

screens.title: Baking Textures and Attributes into Maps
screens.narratorSegment: Procedural HDAs excel at generating attributes — color masks, density fields, curvature, ambient occlusion — but game engines generally prefer texture maps. Baking converts these procedural values into texture files. Use Attribute Transfer or Attribute VOP to generate per-vertex or per-primitive attributes on your mesh, then use Labs Maps Baker or custom baking setups to write those attributes into textures such as AO, curvature, or density masks. A concrete workflow: ensure your mesh has clean UVs via UV Unwrap and UV Layout, create the attribute you want to bake (for instance a moss density mask), run your baker to sample attribute values across UV space and export a grayscale PNG or EXR. A common misconception is to skip UV cleanup and expect good maps — poor UVs produce stretching and seams. Key takeaway: bake only the necessary maps, verify UVs first, and choose formats appropriate for the engine and map type (use EXR for high precision when needed). Baking moves rich procedural data into the engine as lightweight, G P U-friendly assets. In practical terms, turn procedural attributes into engine-ready texture maps.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Create clean UVs, generate attributes, and bake them into texture maps so procedural detail becomes engine-efficient assets.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Baking Attributes
Baking Workflow
  1. Ensure clean UVs with UV Unwrap / UV Layout.
  2. Create the procedural attribute (moss density, curvature, AO).
  3. Use Labs Maps Baker or Attribute VOP/Transfer to sample and bake to texture.
  4. Export maps as PNG/EXR for engine import and test them in materials.
Concrete Example
Generate a moss density attribute on rock faces, verify UVs, then bake the attribute to a grayscale PNG. Use that texture in the engine as a mask to blend moss materials without expensive runtime calculations.
Common Mistake

Baking before fixing UVs produces distorted maps; always check UV layout and padding before baking for mipmapping.

screens.title: Designing HDAs for Game Engines: Modularity, Parameters, and LODs
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a game-ready HDA is both a technical and UX design task. Start by making the HDA modular: each HDA should perform a single clear job — a building segment, a prop, or a terrain detail. This allows different pieces to have separate budgets and export paths. Next, expose only essential parameters and organize them logically; avoid exposing low-level nodes that let users inadvertently increase cost beyond the target budget. Provide a small LOD system inside the HDA: for example, include a PolyReduce node chained into a LOD branch and promote the target percentage or direct LOD buttons so artists can bake multiple LODs easily. Also include an option to output simplified collision geometry, either via a separate, lower-poly chain or by generating convex hulls automatically. A common misconception is to overload an HDA with too many features; this reduces clarity and increases the chance of costly settings. HDA Structure Checklist

Design with constraints: modular HDAs with limited, documented parameters lead to predictable engine assets.

screens.title: Walkthrough: Optimize and Pre-Bake cohortia_simple_box HDA
screens.narratorSegment: This guided walkthrough follows the hands-on activity in the chapter. Start by opening your cohortia_simple_box HDA and dive inside to the SOP chain. First, insert a PolyReduce node after the Normal SOP and set a conservative Target Percentage, for example fifty percent; this reduces triangle count while preserving form. Expose that parameter on the HDA so artists can dial it later. Next, add a Clean SOP after PolyReduce and enable Remove Unused Groups and Remove Degenerate Geometry; this fixes artifacts and trims invisible data. Then add a ROP Geometry Output node connected to the Clean SOP, set the Output File to a clear path such as $HIP/geo/cohortia_simple_box_baked. fbx, and set SOP Path to the Clean SOP. Use this ROP to export an FBX for the engine. As an alternative or complement, place a File Cache node after Clean and write $HIP/cache/cohortia_simple_box_cache.$F. bgeo. sc to disk. Saving to disk caches the heavy compute and speeds iteration. A common mistake is exporting before cleaning and deleting attributes; always run Clean and Attribute Delete to ensure small, consistent exports. Final step: save the HDA type definition so your exported parameters remain available for future artists. Reflect: did the exported file stay within your platform budget?

screens.title: Material Assignment and Exporting Masks
screens.narratorSegment: Material assignment and mask baking are an important bridge between Houdini and the engine. Provide robust ways to assign materials by outputting specific groups or material ID attributes that correspond to engine material indices. Alternatively, bake material masks as textures so the engine can blend materials based on texture maps. A practical example: output groups named mat_brick and mat_mortar or create a primitive attribute carrying material ID; then your engine importer can assign the correct materials at import automatically. When baking masks, ensure your UVs are non-overlapping for charts that need unique texel space, or accept tiling for repetitive materials. A misconception is to rely on per-primitive color for material assignment — many engines prefer explicit material slots or texture maps. Key takeaway: design your HDA to output either explicit material groups/IDs or baked masks so materials can be consistently applied in the engine pipeline. This reduces manual remapping and preserves consistent visuals across platforms. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why performance must be a first-class concern when authoring Houdini Digital Assets for games. We’ll define the core metrics you will monitor — polygon count, draw calls, and texture memory — and show how a procedural HDA can unintentionally exceed budgets if nodes like subdivision, many booleans, or dense VDB conversions are used without restraint. You will see practical strategies for streamlining node graphs, using PolyReduce and Clean to reduce geometry and attribute overhead, and how to bake or cache stable outputs with ROP Geometry Output and File Cache to avoid expensive cooks at runtime. We’ll also cover baking attribute maps — for example turning a procedural moss density attribute into a grayscale texture — and why clean UVs and normals matter before exporting to a game engine. Finally, we’ll outline HDA design best practices: modularity, clear parameters, LOD support, and providing collision geometry. By the end you’ll understand both the techniques and the trade-offs needed to produce HDAs that are flexible for artists and light enough for real-time engines.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify the primary performance metrics that matter for real-time assets, optimize HDA internals to reduce geometry and attribute overhead, and bake stable outputs for game engines. You’ll learn to use PolyReduce, Clean, Fuse, and Attribute Delete to shape geometry and memory usage, and you’ll practice exporting baked geometry using ROP Geometry Output or File Cache for reliable engine imports. You’ll also learn how to bake attribute-driven masks and utility maps so procedural data can become practical texture inputs in the engine. Each objective pairs a technical skill with a practical reason: reducing polygons keeps frame rates steady; baking avoids expensive cooks inside the engine; and clean UVs plus proper normals make materials behave predictably. As you practice, you’ll compare common mistakes — like overusing subdivide nodes — with better alternatives so you build an HDA that balances control and runtime cost.

This continuation focuses on practical outcomes: creating modular HDAs that expose only necessary parameters, designing LODs, providing collision geometry, and documenting usage so other team members can reuse your tools. You will learn how to break complex assets into smaller HDAs for buildings, props, and terrain elements so each piece can be optimized separately. We’ll practice assigning material groups or baking masks to make engine material setup straightforward, and explore simple ways to generate collision meshes inside an HDA. You will also be guided to adopt a performance budget mindset: choose target polygon counts and draw-call limits for your platform and design your HDA to remain within those bounds. Finally, you’ll be encouraged to document parameters and intended use cases, because clear documentation saves time and reduces misuse in a production pipeline.

Performance for game assets is not an abstract goal — it is a set of measurable constraints. Polygon count is the total number of polygons your mesh contains and directly affects G P U throughput. Draw calls are how many times the C P U needs to instruct the G P U to render geometry; many separate meshes or material changes increase draw calls. Texture memory is the combined size of your texture maps and controls G P U memory usage. When designing an HDA, think in budgets: an HDA that outputs many separate primitives or high-resolution textures will consume more of these limits. A concrete example: a procedural tree HDA that generates highly detailed leaves with per-leaf meshes will skyrocket poly count and draw calls compared to a card-based sprite solution. A common misconception is assuming procedural flexibility automatically translates to runtime performance — it does not. Procedural generation is powerful while authoring, but what matters at runtime is the final baked geometry and assets the engine receives. Key takeaway: always measure the outputs your HDA produces in terms of triangles, number of objects/material groups, and texture sizes, and set target values that match your platform. A practical check is to ask: can I reduce the mesh or combine material groups without losing the visual goal? That question guides the optimization choices you’ll make later in the workflow.

Optimizing an HDA begins with a disciplined pass through its internal network. Start by identifying redundant or unused nodes: delete unnecessary SOPs, merge equivalent flows, and remove attributes that are no longer used. A useful process is: first profile the HDA by observing cook times and the viewport's geometry stats; second, replace expensive nodes or reduce their parameters (for example reduce Subdivide iterations); third, promote important controls like the PolyReduce target to the HDA interface so artists can trade quality for performance. A concrete example: if your HDA performs multiple overlapping boolean operations, try precomputing the boolean result in a cached branch and using a single, cleaned output for all subsequent steps. Another practical step is attribute hygiene — use Attribute Delete to strip attributes like temporary masks or per-point IDs before exporting. A common misconception is believing that more nodes always give more control; in practice, a dense graph with many intermediate results slows cooks and complicates debugging. Key takeaway: optimize both the topology of the node graph and the data it carries by pruning nodes and attributes, and provide a small set of well-documented parameters to control remaining detail.

PolyReduce is your primary tool for lowering polygon count while attempting to preserve silhouette and visual fidelity. It is optimal when you need to decimate dense meshes intelligently. However, it is not a one-stop solution: Fuse is useful to merge overlapping points and reduce vertex count, while Clean removes unused groups, attributes, and degenerate geometry that can silently bloat exports. Attribute Delete targets memory and file size by removing attributes that the game engine will not use. A concrete example: after decimating a scanned rock with PolyReduce, you should run Fuse to collapse nearly coincident points created by the simplification, run Clean to remove degenerate primitives, and then Attribute Delete to remove scan-specific attributes like raw color or per-vertex IDs. A common misconception is to over-rely on PolyReduce for all optimization; PolyReduce changes topology and can destroy UV layouts if not configured properly. Key takeaway: use PolyReduce to control triangle budgets, then use Fuse, Clean, and Attribute Delete as a final hygiene pass to ensure exports are compact and engine-friendly. When you expose PolyReduce settings as an HDA parameter, document acceptable ranges so artists don’t exceed platform budgets.

Baking is the practice of converting dynamic or expensive procedural results into static files that the engine can load quickly. Houdini provides the ROP Geometry Output node to export geometry directly to formats like FBX and the File Cache node to save networks as. bgeo. sc or other formats. A robust bake architecture separates outputs by purpose: visual mesh, collision mesh, and LOD meshes should each have a dedicated ROP or cache path. For example, connect the cleaned HDA output to a ROP Geometry Output node named with suffixes like _mesh, _collision, or _lod1 so your pipeline can import each file into the engine. Use File Cache for internal iteration — if an HDA takes 30 seconds to cook, caching that result to disk yields rapid iteration and avoids re-cooking heavy operations. A common misconception is that baking removes the need for version control; on the contrary, you should version baked outputs and keep the HDA definition under control too. Key takeaway: design bake outputs explicitly, separate functional exports, and automate file naming. This makes importing into the engine predictable and fast for runtime use.

Automation reduces human error when setting up exports. The chapter includes a simple Python pattern to create a geometry container, a sphere and a null, and hook the sphere into the null. You can adapt this style to create a ROP or File Cache node and set its parameters programmatically. For example, a script that creates a geo container and inside it creates an FBX ROP lets you standardize output paths and SOP paths across many HDAs. A misconception is believing automation replaces thinking; instead, automation enforces consistent naming and reduces tedious setup. Concretely, you might create a script that: creates the geo node, builds the internal chain up to the Clean SOP, creates a ROP Geometry Output node, sets Output File to a predictable path, and triggers render. This ensures every artist exports with the same settings and reduces mistakes like forgetting to set the SOP Path. The takeaway: use small scripts to standardize exports but keep the logic simple and well-documented so others can adapt it without breaking pipeline conventions. Procedural HDAs excel at generating attributes — color masks, density fields, curvature, ambient occlusion — but game engines generally prefer texture maps. Baking converts these procedural values into texture files.
